mainTopic: Which birds are kosher: why the listed non-kosher birds (עורב, פרס and עזניה, נשר) do not forbid every bird with fewer signs, and why the Torah mentions doves
overview: The גמרא tests whether we can build a general rule from the birds the Torah lists as non-kosher. It first suggests learning from the עורב, which has two signs yet is forbidden, that every two-sign bird is forbidden. It rejects this: then the Torah would not need to list the פרס and עזניה, which have only one sign. Next it suggests learning from the פרס and עזניה that every one-sign bird is forbidden. It rejects this too: then the Torah would not need the נשר, which has no signs. So the נשר teaches that a bird with even one sign is kosher, unless the Torah names it. The גמרא asks whether the פרס and עזניה are 'two verses that come as one,' which cannot teach a rule. It answers with traditions about how the four signs are spread among the 24 non-kosher birds: one of the pair has a sign that no other listed bird has, so a rule really could have been learned. Finally the גמרא asks why the Torah mentions doves. רב עוקבא בר חמא says they are mentioned for קרבנות, and רב נחמן begins a second answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why not learn a general rule from the crow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that since the עורב has two signs and is still not kosher, every bird with only two signs should be non-kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us learn from the crow: just as the crow has two signs and is not kosher, so too any bird with only two signs is not kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge. It suggests using the עורב as a model to forbid every bird that has only two kosher signs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The עורב is listed in the Torah as non-kosher even though it has two signs. The challenge says: turn that one case into a general rule. If that works, many more birds would be forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us learn (derive a rule from a case)
Crow, a non-kosher bird listed in the Torah
Just as ... so too: the pattern for comparing cases
Two (here, two kosher signs)

phrases.english: But let us learn from the crow:
Just as there, with two signs, it is not kosher,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the crow. It has two of the kosher signs of a bird, yet the Torah forbids it.

phrases.english: so too any bird with two signs is not kosher?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge about building a general rule from the listed non-kosher birds.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the listed non-kosher birds are only individual cases and not a general rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The עורב has two signs and is still forbidden, so maybe every two-sign bird should be forbidden.

steps.title: Then why list the פרס and עזניה?
steps.stepSummary: If every bird with two signs were forbidden, the Torah would not need to list the פרס and עזניה, which have only one sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why did the Torah need to write the פרס and עזניה? Now that we do not eat a bird with two signs, do we need to be told about birds with only one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows that learning from the עורב would make the Torah's listing of the פרס and עזניה pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פרס and עזניה have only one sign each. If two signs were already not enough, a bird with one sign would obviously be forbidden, and the Torah would not need to mention them. Since the Torah did mention them, we cannot make a general rule from the עורב.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher bird listed in the Torah, with one sign
A non-kosher bird listed in the Torah, with one sign
The Merciful One: a name for ה׳ as the author of the Torah
Why do I need it? Asking why a verse is not extra
Is it necessary? Meaning it should be obvious

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say the עורב is kosher. The עורב stays forbidden. The point is only that we cannot stretch its rule to every other bird with two signs.

phrases.english: If so, the peres and the ozniyya
that the Merciful One wrote, why do I need them?

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא דְּאִית לֵיהּ תְּרֵי לָא אָכְלִינַן,
phrases.english: Now, if a bird that has two signs we do not eat,
is it necessary to say so for one that has only one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, פֶּרֶס וְעׇזְנִיָּה דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא לְמָה לִי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that a verse would be unnecessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We could forbid every two-sign bird by learning from the עורב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The listing of the פרס and עזניה shows that the עורב cannot be made into a general rule.

steps.title: Why not learn a rule from the פרס and עזניה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests learning from the פרס and עזניה that every bird with only one sign is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let us learn from the פרס and עזניה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new, smaller challenge. If not two signs, then maybe at least every bird with only one sign is forbidden, like the פרס and עזניה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 showed the Torah needed to list one-sign birds. So now the challenge uses those one-sign birds as the model, to forbid all birds with only one sign.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us learn (another word for deriving a rule)

phrases.english: But let us learn from the peres and ozniyya?
phrases.notes: He means: every bird with only one sign should be forbidden, just like these two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the birds from step 2's answer as a new model for a general rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that birds with one sign might be kosher
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פרס and עזניה have one sign and are forbidden, so maybe every one-sign bird is forbidden.

steps.title: The נשר shows only a bird with no signs is automatically forbidden
steps.stepSummary: If every one-sign bird were forbidden, the Torah would not need to list the נשר, which has no signs. So the נשר teaches that a bird with even one sign may be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why did the Torah need to write the נשר? Now that we do not eat a bird with one sign, do we need to be told about a bird with none? Rather, the נשר, which has no signs, is what you may not eat. But a bird that has one sign, you may eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with the same kind of reasoning. Listing the נשר would be pointless if one-sign birds were already forbidden, so the Torah must be teaching that only birds with no signs are forbidden as a rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The נשר has no kosher signs at all. If one sign were not enough, a bird with none would obviously be forbidden. So the mention of the נשר teaches the opposite: a bird with one sign is permitted, except for the birds the Torah lists by name.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher bird listed in the Torah, with no kosher signs
Now: introducing a 'how much more so' argument
At all
It has / it does not have

steps.whatToRemember: Order of the birds: the עורב has two signs, the פרס and עזניה have one, and the נשר has none. Since the Torah needed to list the נשר, a bird with even one sign is kosher unless the Torah names it.

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן, נֶשֶׁר דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: If so, the nesher that the Merciful One wrote, why do I need it?

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא דְּאִית לֵיהּ חַד לָא אָכְלִינַן,
phrases.english: Now, if a bird that has one sign we do not eat,
is it necessary to say so for one that has none at all?
Rather, the nesher, which has none at all,
that is what you may not eat;
but one that has one sign, eat it.
phrases.notes: This leaves out birds the Torah lists by name, like the פרס and עזניה. Those stay forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נֶשֶׁר דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 3 and states the rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that a verse would be unnecessary, then drawing the rule from it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every one-sign bird is forbidden, learned from the פרס and עזניה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a bird with no signs is forbidden as a general rule; a bird with one sign may be eaten.

steps.title: Why would we ever learn from two verses that come as one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: without the נשר, how could we have learned from the פרס and עזניה at all? Two verses that teach the same thing do not teach a general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, the reason is that the Merciful One wrote נשר. Without that, I would have said: learn from the פרס and עזניה? They are two verses that come as one, and two verses that come as one do not teach.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 4. That answer assumed we would have learned from the פרס and עזניה, but there is a rule that such a pair cannot teach anything for other cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said the נשר was needed to block a rule learned from the פרס and עזניה. But by the rule of שני כתובין הבאין כאחד, two cases that teach the same law cannot be applied to other cases. So the rule was already blocked, and the נשר seems unnecessary for that.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason
I would have thought (the first assumption)
Two verses that come as one: two cases that teach the same law
They do not teach (no general rule can be learned from them)

steps.confusionAlert: The rule of שני כתובין הבאין כאחד says: if the Torah had to state a law twice, that shows the law is NOT a general rule. Otherwise one case would have been enough.

phrases.english: But then, the reason is that the Merciful One wrote nesher,
so if not for that, I would have said:
learn from the peres and ozniyya?
The peres and ozniyya are
two verses that come as one,
phrases.notes: Both birds have only one sign and are forbidden, so they seem to teach the very same thing.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁנֵי כְּתוּבִין הַבָּאִין כְּאֶחָד אֵין מְלַמְּדִין.
phrases.english: and two verses that come as one do not teach.

steps.kashyaTarget: Step 4's claim that the נשר was needed to stop us from learning from the פרס and עזניה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פרס and עזניה are שני כתובין הבאין כאחד, which cannot teach a general rule anyway.

steps.title: Each bird has a different sign, so they are not a matching pair
steps.stepSummary: By tradition, the sign the פרס has, the עזניה lacks, and the other way around. So they teach two different things and are not 'two verses that come as one.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned as a tradition that the sign present in this one is missing in that one, and the sign present in that one is missing in this one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 5 with a known tradition about the two birds. Because each has a different sign, they are not a repeated lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each bird teaches its own lesson: a bird with only the פרס's sign is forbidden, and a bird with only the עזניה's sign is forbidden. Since they are not the same, the rule of שני כתובין does not apply. So without the נשר we really would have forbidden one-sign birds, and the נשר is needed after all.

keyTerms.meaning: We have a tradition (passed down, not taken from a verse)
There is / there is not
In this one

steps.whatToRemember: For now: the פרס and עזניה each have a different single sign, so they seem able to teach a rule. The next step challenges this, and step 8 settles it.

phrases.english: It is learned by tradition: what is in this one is not in that one,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the פרס and 'that one' is the עזניה. Each has a different one of the kosher signs.

phrases.english: and what is in that one is not in this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5 and keeps step 4's reasoning in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case differently (the two birds are not the same)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פרס and עזניה teach the same thing, so they could not teach a rule and the נשר would not be needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each has a different sign, so they could have taught a rule, and the נשר was needed to permit one-sign birds.

steps.title: Surely the one sign of the פרס and עזניה shows up in other birds too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that among 24 non-kosher birds, the single sign found in the פרס or the עזניה must also appear in some other bird. If so, they are 'two verses that come as one' and cannot teach a rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look, there are twenty-four non-kosher birds. It is impossible that the one sign found in these birds is not found in any of those other birds. So they become two verses that come as one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 6. Even if the פרס and עזניה have different signs, each sign is probably shared by some other non-kosher bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6 the גמרא said the פרס and עזניה each teach something different. Now it says: with 24 birds on the list, the פרס's sign surely appears in another listed bird, and so does the עזניה's sign. Then each lesson is taught twice, which makes it 'two verses that come as one,' and no general rule can be learned from them.

keyTerms.meaning: Look, since it is so. It opens an argument built on known facts.
Non-kosher birds
It is impossible

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה עוֹפוֹת טְמֵאִים הָווּ,
phrases.english: Look, there are twenty-four non-kosher birds,
it is impossible that the one sign found in these
phrases.notes: 'These' means the פרס and the עזניה.

phrases.english: is not found in those,
phrases.notes: 'Those' means the other birds on the list.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָווּ לְהוּ שְׁנֵי כְּתוּבִים הַבָּאִים כְּאֶחָד.
phrases.english: and so they are two verses that come as one.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדֵי עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה עוֹפוֹת טְמֵאִים הָווּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 6 by saying each sign is surely repeated in another bird.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 6 that the פרס and עזניה are not 'two verses that come as one.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With 24 birds, each single sign must appear in at least one more bird, so each lesson is doubled and cannot become a general rule.

steps.title: A tradition about the signs shows the נשר is still needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from a tradition: there are 24 non-kosher birds and four signs. Three signs are spread among all the birds, but the fourth sign is found only in the פרס or the עזניה and in no other listed bird. So one might have learned from it that a one-sign bird is forbidden, and the Torah wrote נשר to block that.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a tradition: there are twenty-four non-kosher birds and four signs. Three signs come up in all of them. Twenty of them, three each. Two in the crow. One in the פרס and one in the עזניה, and what this one has, that one lacks. You might say, learn a rule from it. So the Torah wrote 'נשר': it is the נשר, which has no sign at all, that you may not eat. But if a bird has one sign, eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a known tradition about how the four signs are spread among the non-kosher birds. One of the two, the פרס or the עזניה, has a sign that no other non-kosher bird has, so the נשר is needed after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tradition shows the signs are not spread the way step 7 assumed. Three signs recur among all the birds, but the fourth sign appears only in one of the pair (פרס or עזניה), and in no other non-kosher bird. That lone case is not 'two verses that come as one,' so we could have learned from it that a bird with only that sign is forbidden. That is why the Torah lists the נשר, which has no signs, to teach that only a bird with no signs is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Signs that show whether a bird is kosher
Come back, recur (here, signs that appear again and again among the birds)
You might have said. It introduces a mistaken idea that the Torah comes to block.

steps.whatToRemember: The נשר, which has no signs, teaches that only a bird with no kosher signs at all is forbidden. A bird with even one sign may be eaten.

phrases.english: We have a tradition:
there are twenty-four non-kosher birds,
and four signs.
Three signs come up in all of them,
twenty of them, three each,
and two in the crow,
one in the פרס and one in the עזניה,
what is in this one is not in that one.
You might say: let us learn a rule from it.
phrases.notes: He means: learn from the פרס and עזניה that any bird with one sign is forbidden.

phrases.english: So the Merciful One wrote 'נשר',
the נשר, which has no sign at all,
is the one you may not eat,

phrases.aramaic: הָא אִיכָּא דְּאִית לֵיהּ חַד – אֱכוֹל.
phrases.english: but if there is one that has one sign, eat it.

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּמִירִי: עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה עוֹפוֹת טְמֵאִים הָווּ, וְאַרְבָּעָה סִימָנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 with a tradition about how the signs are spread among the birds.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual tradition about the birds' signs
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sign of the פרס and the sign of the עזניה are each repeated in other birds, so no rule could be learned from them.
steps.terutzMaskana: By tradition, one of them has a sign found in no other non-kosher bird. A rule could have been learned from it, so the נשר is needed to teach that a bird with one sign may be eaten.

steps.title: Then why does the Torah mention the doves?
steps.stepSummary: If even one sign makes a bird kosher, why does the Torah need to mention doves, which are kosher birds?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, why do I need the doves that the Merciful One wrote?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question based on the conclusion of step 8. If the rule is clear, the Torah's mention of doves seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 concluded that any bird with even one sign is kosher. Doves are obviously kosher under that rule. So what does the Torah gain by mentioning them?

keyTerms.meaning: Doves (turtledoves)

phrases.english: But then, the doves that the Merciful One wrote,
why do I need them?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, תּוֹרִין דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the conclusion of step 8 to ask why another פסוק is needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one sign is enough for a bird to be kosher, mentioning a fully kosher bird like the dove teaches nothing.

steps.title: The doves are mentioned for קרבנות
steps.stepSummary: רב עוקבא בר חמא answers that the doves are not mentioned to show they are kosher. They are mentioned to teach that they are used for a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עוקבא בר חמא said: For a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב עוקבא בר חמא answers the question of step 9. The doves teach a law about קרבנות, not about kosher food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed the Torah mentioned doves to tell us they are kosher. רב עוקבא בר חמא says that is not the purpose. They are mentioned because they are fit to be brought as a קרבן, so the mention is not wasted.

keyTerms.meaning: An offering brought in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: רב עוקבא בר חמא said:
For a קרבן.
phrases.notes: He means the doves are mentioned to teach about bringing them as a קרבן, not to show they are kosher.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב עוּקְבָא בַּר חָמָא: לְקׇרְבָּן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirects the פסוק to a different purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Torah mentioned doves to teach that they are kosher, which would be unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The doves are mentioned for the laws of קרבנות.

steps.title: רב נחמן begins a different answer
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן is introduced as giving another answer about why the doves are mentioned. His words continue in the next part of the daf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a second answer to the question about the doves. רב נחמן's actual answer comes right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the opening of רב נחמן's statement appears here. It signals another way of explaining why the Torah needed to mention doves, different from רב עוקבא בר חמא's answer about קרבנות.

phrases.english: רב נחמן said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a second answer to the question of step 9, besides step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative answer (its content continues beyond this text)
